generatedProse.concept-context: Behind much team conflict lie real differences in how people approach work: some push a bold idea, others urge caution, and both can be right in part. Seeing the person behind the position, rather than only the position, lets you respond to what is actually driving a disagreement. Reflecting on that with a judgement, rather than a bare description of events, is itself a skill that employers value.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students in a team where two members are arguing hard over how to present the results, two days before the deadline.

{{learner-a}} finds the row stressful and stays quiet, hoping it will pass. Asked later to reflect, {{learner-a}} writes that 'there was a disagreement but we sorted it in the end'. The conflict was neither helped nor understood, and the reflection only describes what happened. Nothing was learned that could be carried into the next team.

{{learner-b}} sees that one member wants something bold and the other wants something safe, and that both have a point. {{learner-b}} acknowledges each view, then proposes keeping the clear, careful version while adding one bold element from the other side. Reflecting afterwards, {{learner-b}} writes that stepping in early, and naming the strengths on both sides, was what held the team together, and would do so again. That is a judgement, and it names a skill worth keeping.

Both students saw the same argument. Only {{learner-b}} resolved it and learned something sayable from it.
generatedProse.summary: Handling conflict in any subject starts with recognising the difference behind it. Reflecting well means judging your own performance, not just describing events, and naming what you have gained. You can now do both, and explain the lasting value of presenting and working in teams. With authority, collaboration and reflection in place, you are ready to present and work in groups like a capable graduate.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s reflection a judgement rather than a description?

items.text: It said what {{learner-b}} did, why it worked, and what {{learner-b}} would do again.
It gave a fuller account of what happened in the meeting.
It named the other team members and their roles.

feedback.correct: That's right. {{learner-b}} weighed their own actions and drew a lesson, which is more than description.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what the reflection concluded about {{learner-b}}'s own performance, not how much it described.
feedback.incorrectFinal: It was a judgement because it weighed what {{learner-b}} did, why it worked, and what {{learner-b}} would repeat. A fuller or longer account of events is still description.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
